title: The First Electronic Computers
summary: Between 1936 and 1949 the modern computer was invented - Turing's idea of a universal machine, Zuse's relay computer, Colossus and ENIAC with their thousands of vacuum tubes, and the stored-program design that every computer since has used.
markdown:
## Turing's universal machine (1936) Before anyone built an electronic computer, **Alan Turing** worked out what any computer could and could not do. In a 1936 paper he imagined a very simple machine: - an endless **tape** divided into squares, each holding one symbol; - a **head** that reads one square, writes a symbol, and moves left or right; - a small table of **rules**: "in state 3, if you read a 1, write 0, move right, go to state 5". He showed that this simple machine can calculate anything that can be calculated at all, and that one such machine - a **universal** machine - can read the rules of any other machine from its tape and imitate it. That is the idea of a computer that runs any program: the program is just more data on the tape. Every computer since, including your phone, is "Turing-complete": given enough memory and time, it can compute anything any other computer can. They differ in speed, not in what is possible. ## Relays, tubes and wartime The first working computers were built during the Second World War, from the switches available then: | Switch | How it works | Speed | |---|---|---| | **Relay** | An electromagnet pulls a metal contact closed. It clicks | About 10 switches a second | | **Vacuum tube** (valve) | A glowing glass tube; a voltage on a grid lets current through or not | Thousands a second, but hot, large and they burned out | | **Transistor** (from 1947) | A tiny piece of silicon, no moving parts | Billions a second today | | Year | Computer | Who and where | What was new | |---|---|---|---| | 1941 | **Z3** | Konrad Zuse, Berlin | The first working programmable, fully automatic computer. Built from about 2,600 relays, and it already used **binary** | | 1943-44 | **Colossus** | Tommy Flowers, Bletchley Park, UK | Electronic (vacuum tubes), built to break German codes. Kept secret until the 1970s | | 1945 | **ENIAC** | Eckert and Mauchly, University of Pennsylvania | About 18,000 vacuum tubes, 27 tonnes, a whole room. Used decimal, not binary. Programmed by **rewiring** cables and setting switches, which took days | The first people to program ENIAC were six women - Kay McNulty, Betty Jennings, Betty Snyder, Marlyn Wescoff, Fran Bilas and Ruth Lichterman - who worked out how to set up its cables and switches from the circuit diagrams, with no manual and no programming language. ## The stored-program idea Rewiring a machine for every new problem was slow. In 1945 **John von Neumann** wrote a report describing a better design (building on Eckert and Mauchly's work): keep the **program in the same memory as the data**. Then loading a new program is as quick as reading new numbers, and a program can even work on other programs. ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph Memory P["Instructions"] D["Data"] end CPU["CPU
control unit + arithmetic"] <--> Memory IN["Input"] --> CPU CPU --> OUT["Output"] ``` This is called the **von Neumann architecture**, and nearly every computer since works this way. The CPU fetches an instruction from memory, carries it out, then fetches the next one. You will step through this cycle yourself in lesson 4.04. | Year | Computer | Why it matters | |---|---|---| | 1948 | **Manchester Baby** (UK) | The first computer to run a program stored in its own electronic memory, on 21 June 1948 | | 1949 | **EDSAC** (Cambridge, UK) | The first practical stored-program computer in regular use. Its "initial orders" let people write instructions as letters and numbers instead of raw binary: an early step towards assembly language (lesson 5.01) | > [!info] The first "bug" > In 1947 the team working on the Harvard Mark II relay computer found a moth stuck in a relay, and taped it into their logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found". The word "bug" for a fault was older than that, but the moth made the story famous. Grace Hopper, who told the story often, comes back in lesson 5.02. ## How big, how fast ENIAC could do about **5,000 additions a second**. A phone today does tens of **billions** of operations a second, uses a few watts instead of 150 kilowatts, and fits in a pocket. The ideas, though - binary, stored programs, fetch and execute - are the ones from these few years. ## Check yourself ```quiz ? What did Turing's 1936 paper show? - How to build a reliable vacuum tube + That one universal machine can run any program - How to break the Enigma code > A simple "universal" machine can follow the rules of any other machine, because the program is just more data for it to read. That is the idea behind every general-purpose computer. ? What problem did the stored-program design solve? - Computers were too heavy to move + Changing the program meant rewiring by hand - Computers could not use binary numbers > ENIAC had to be rewired for every new problem; storing the program in memory made changing it as easy as loading data. Nearly every computer since the Manchester Baby (1948) works this way. ? Which of these was built from relays? - ENIAC + The Z3 - Colossus > Zuse's Z3 used about 2,600 relays. Colossus and ENIAC used vacuum tubes. ```

cards.a:
That one universal machine can run any program

A simple "universal" machine can follow the rules of any other machine, because the program is just more data for it to read. That is the idea behind every general-purpose computer.

cards.q: What problem did the stored-program design solve?
cards.a:
Changing the program meant rewiring by hand

ENIAC had to be rewired for every new problem; storing the program in memory made changing it as easy as loading data. Nearly every computer since the Manchester Baby (1948) works this way.

cards.q: Which of these was built from relays?
cards.a:
The Z3

Zuse's Z3 used about 2,600 relays. Colossus and ENIAC used vacuum tubes.
